sources.entry: pmu-tools - Runs the TMA tree on Linux from the spreadsheet and states why multiplexed levels mislead on short or varied workloads.

summary.one_liner: A collection of Python tools and a C library for Intel CPU performance profiling on Linux perf, centered on the toplev top-down (TMA) bottleneck analyzer.
summary.what_it_does: The repository bundles several tools for collecting and analyzing Intel CPU performance counters through Linux perf. toplev implements the TopDown/TopDown2 methodology to identify micro-architectural bottlenecks for a workload, with options for levels, node metrics, a bottlenecks view, drilldown with minimal multiplexing, and interval CSV output. ocperf wraps perf with full Intel core event lists using symbolic names, and it can be used as a Python library. ucevent handles uncore events, and jevents is a C library for resolving named Intel events to perf_event_attr. The README also mentions cputop for topology and hybrid core queries, msr and pci for register access, and plotting or XLSX spreadsheet generation for post-processing interval measurements. The tools are run from the source directory and download Intel event lists on first run.
use_cases: Find CPU bottlenecks in a program with top-down analysis
Generate a spreadsheet or charts of CPU metrics
Measure a workload with symbolic Intel event names
Collect interval CSV performance data for a whole system
Measure uncore events such as memory or interconnect counters
Query CPU topology or pin workloads to specific cores
how_to_run: pip install -r requirements.txt   (optional, for plots and XLSX output)
cd jevents && make   (optional, to build the jevents C library)
stack: Optional: external Python libraries from requirements.txt for plots and XLSX
notable: toplev implements the TopDown / TopDown2 methodology and is updated to recent TMA model versions
Bottlenecks view summarizes the TMA tree into a short list of performance issues
--drilldown reruns the workload with minimal multiplexing to find the critical bottleneck
Runs out of the source directory with no install step for most tools
caveats: Requires Intel CPUs; needs a reasonably recent kernel and perf tools for newer CPU models
Needs internet access on first run to download Intel event lists; later runs can be offline
Plots and XLSX spreadsheets need extra Python packages
Some older tools such as simple-pebs are no longer supported
Multiplexing counters can introduce measurement errors, as the README notes for -NB runs
summary.license: GPLv2 for ocperf, toplev, ucevent, parser; modified BSD for jevents
keywords: find why my code is slow
